clue.text: Screen actor finally brought before court claims to be revolutionary

indicators.note: what comes finally is at the very end, so only the closing letter is kept
a revolution turns things right round, so each piece is flipped end to end

blocks.note: the final letter of actor
someone up before the magistrate is brought before court
as in 'he had it that...', meaning he claimed

explanation.surface: A film star is hauled into the dock, insisting they are a revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screen' looks like cinema, chiming with the actor, but it is a curtain. 'Up before the court' is the idiom for facing a judge, and the reversal acts on each half separately rather than on the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Purdah is the curtain or practice of screening women from men or strangers in some Muslim and Hindu societies.

clue.text: Defensive line perhaps royal equerry uttered

indicators.note: something uttered is spoken, so we want a word that is said the same way

blocks.note: an equerry is an officer attending a royal, so an aide at the palace

explanation.surface: A courtier lets slip a remark that sounds like part of a sports team's defence.
explanation.walkthrough: An equerry is a member of the royal household, so a palace aide; run those two words together and they sound like the fence of stakes.
explanation.definitionFit: A palisade is a fence of pointed wooden stakes built as a fortification, one example of a defensive barrier.

clue.text: Neglect a suspect supporting essentially corrupt figure

indicators.note: as an adjective, suspect means dubious or not genuine, so the letters are not to be trusted in their order
the essence of a word is its heart, so only its central letter is kept
in a down clue, a piece supporting another sits beneath it

blocks.note: the central letter of corrupt
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A shady character is accused of ignoring a crooked official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' hides at the end looking like a person; it is a geometric shape. The rearranged letters sit under the R in the down grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectangle is a four-sided plane shape with right angles, a basic example of a geometric figure.

clue.text: Hints those dull adverts upset hosts

indicators.note: to host is to have guests inside, so the run of letters is sitting within the phrase
in a down clue, upset means tipped up, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a run across the last letters of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that boring advertisements have got under the skin of the people presenting them.
explanation.walkthrough: Read thoSE DULL Adverts backwards and the answer appears; 'Hints' is a verb, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To allude is to refer indirectly or suggest something without stating it, so alludes and hints are synonyms as verbs.

clue.text: Travelling south, together with several hundred

indicators.note: things travelling are on the move, so these letters move about

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
and means together with

explanation.surface: A large party heads south as a group.
explanation.walkthrough: Several hundred is ten hundreds here: a thousand is a quantity made of hundreds, which keeps the definition fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A thousand is ten hundreds, so it is literally a number made up of several hundreds counted together.

clue.text: Attractive quality, courage, in one sharing your bed?

blocks.note: hot is slang for sexy or attractive
as in a diamond 'of the first water', of the highest quality
bottle is British slang for nerve or courage

explanation.surface: A lonely-hearts ad lists what is wanted in a bed partner: looks, character and nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: Water as quality comes from gem grading, where the finest diamonds are 'of the first water'; bottle meaning courage is British slang. The question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubber container filled with warm liquid is tucked under the covers at night, a cosy companion in the bed.

clue.text: Relative right to keep answer ambiguous

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside, so one piece is held within the other

blocks.note: a family member
R is the abbreviation for right
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A family member has the right to give a vague reply.
explanation.walkthrough: UNCLE and R together hold the A, slipping it in just before the final R.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unclear is open to more than one reading or not plainly stated, which is what ambiguous means.

clue.text: Throughout day barely overcomes thirst

indicators.note: something bare is stripped of its covering, so the outer letters are removed
in a down clue, coming over something means sitting on top of it

blocks.note: day stripped of its outside letters
to thirst for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: All day long, someone just about manages to resist being thirsty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overcomes' looks like defeat but just places one piece above the other in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'I knew it all along', the word means for the whole time, from start to finish, matching throughout.

clue.text: Gloomy prohibitionist receiving attention

indicators.note: to receive is to take in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a dry is someone who opposes the sale of alcohol
to give someone your ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: A miserable teetotal campaigner is finally getting noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'dry' as a noun is an advocate of banning alcohol, as in the US Prohibition era.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary describes something dull, bleak and depressing, a near synonym for a gloomy mood or day.

clue.text: Musician chap Rod’s shirt I ripped

indicators.note: a ripped garment is torn apart, so the letters are torn up and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged, including the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A performer confesses to tearing the shirt belonging to a fellow called Rod.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-S in Rod's supplies a letter of the fodder; all fourteen letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: A harpsichordist plays the harpsichord, a keyboard instrument with plucked strings, so is one kind of musician.

clue.text: Number, mostly inexperienced, cycling

indicators.note: most of a thing is all but a bit, so the last letter is dropped
a cycle goes round and comes back, so letters from the front are carried round to the end

blocks.note: callow means inexperienced, here without its final letter

explanation.surface: A cyclist is still mostly a novice at the sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is read as 'something that numbs': a local anaesthetic. Moving CAL from the front of CALLO to the back gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A local is short for a local anaesthetic, which numbs one part of the body, so it is literally a numbing agent.

clue.text: New girlfriend originally denied cooking thick orange vegetable

indicators.note: denying is refusing entry, and originally points at the opening letters, so those first letters are refused
cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are mixed and rearranged

blocks.note: the initial letters of each word, which are taken away
the letters before removal

explanation.surface: A new partner refuses to make a stodgy orange vegetable dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thick orange vegetable' reads like a description of a carrot or squash; only the last word defines. Remove N and G from 'thick orange' and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The globe artichoke and Jerusalem artichoke are both plants eaten as vegetables.

clue.text: Fail to keep appointment with comedian

definitions.note: a noun or adjective use, as in stand-up comedian

blocks.note: first meaning: to leave someone waiting on a date
second meaning: a comic who performs solo before a live audience

explanation.surface: Someone misses a meeting with a comic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' belongs to the first definition: you stand someone up, so the phrase needs its object.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand someone up is to not turn up for a date; a stand-up is a solo comic who performs live on stage.

clue.text: Vision, say, of Fury boxing against European

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: fury is intense anger
V for versus, against
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A boxing fan's view of the heavyweight Tyson Fury fighting a European opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyson Fury the boxer is a decoy; Vision is a Marvel superhero, a member of the Avengers team.
explanation.definitionFit: Vision is a synthetic superhero in the Marvel comics and films, one member of that team of costumed heroes.

clue.text: Biscuit, delicacy Republican plugs – it may eventually arrive here

indicators.note: a plug fills a hole from inside, so one letter is stuffed into the next piece

blocks.note: a digestive is a plain British wholemeal biscuit
delicacy in dealing with people is tact
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A snack and a treat are promoted, with a warning about where they will end up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delicacy' tempts you to a food word, but here it means sensitivity. The definition reads with the clue: the biscuit eaten will in time arrive in the gut.
explanation.definitionFit: The alimentary canal is where any swallowed food, a biscuit included, ends up after passing down the gullet.

clue.text: One singing in synch – or is terrible?

indicators.note: the letters are located inside the following words rather than built from them

blocks.note: runs from the end of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: A singer asks whether they are keeping time with the others or making a dreadful noise.
explanation.walkthrough: synCH OR IS TERrible: the dash and spaces are ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A chorister is a member of a choir, especially a church choir, so someone who sings with others.

clue.text: Plant Poles had cultivated

indicators.note: cultivated ground is worked over and turned, so the letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Polish gardeners had been growing a particular flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' suggests Polish people or N and S; it is just eight letters for rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: The asphodel is a lily-family flower, in Greek myth said to cover the meadows of the underworld.

clue.text: Street flashers trying to attract attention!

definitions.text: Street flashers trying to attract attention

blocks.note: surface reading: people exposing themselves in public to shock passers-by
setter's reading: flashing amber globes on poles at British zebra crossings, there to catch drivers' eyes

explanation.walkthrough: These lamps, named after the transport minister Leslie Hore-Belisha, mark pedestrian crossings in Britain; 'flashers' is innocent once you see they blink.
explanation.definitionFit: The amber globes blink constantly at the roadside precisely so motorists notice a pedestrian crossing ahead.

clue.text: Sign golfer’s ready to play shows resolve

definitions.note: a phrase describing a situation, not a verb

blocks.note: first meaning: a club pulled from the bag shows the player is about to take a shot
second meaning: to settle or smooth away difficulties

explanation.surface: A golfer gives a signal of readiness and determination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resolve' looks like a noun meaning determination; it is the verb, as in sorting out problems. An iron is a type of golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: To iron out problems is an idiom for settling them, just as ironing removes creases from cloth.

clue.text: MoMA maybe friend enters in the morning

indicators.note: something that enters goes inside, so one piece is put into the other

blocks.note: a crony is a close friend
AM, ante meridiem, before noon

explanation.surface: A pal arrives at the New York art gallery early in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: MoMA stands for the Museum of Modern Art and is pronounced as a word, which is why it is an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: MoMA is formed from the initial letters of Museum of Modern Art and spoken as a word, the textbook case.

clue.text: Sweet daughter put out by comparatively stupid son

indicators.note: putting something out is ejecting it, so that letter is thrown out

blocks.note: daft means stupid, so more stupid is dafter
D is the abbreviation for daughter, the letter removed
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A lovely daughter is upset by a brother who is even sillier than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like an adjective describing the daughter, but it is the British noun for dessert; afters is informal British for the pudding course.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a sweet is the dessert course, and afters is the casual word for what comes after the main meal.

clue.text: Enthusiasm of extra on EastEnders

indicators.note: EastEnders is a BBC soap set in London's East End, so the word is said in a Cockney accent

blocks.note: further means extra, and Cockney speech turns its TH into a V

explanation.surface: An extra in the long-running soap is very keen.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a British TV soap set among Cockneys, who often say V for TH, so 'further' comes out as 'furver'. 'Extra' tempts as a TV bit-part player.
explanation.definitionFit: Fervour is intense passion or zeal for something, a close synonym of enthusiasm.

clue.text: Outsiders excluded from acclaimed institute

indicators.note: the outsiders are the edge letters, and excluding them leaves only the inside

blocks.note: something acclaimed is praised

explanation.surface: Non-members are kept out of a prestigious academy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Institute' looks like a noun for the academy; it is the verb, to start something up, as in raising an objection.
explanation.definitionFit: To institute proceedings or a question is to set it going, and to raise one means to bring it up and start it.

clue.text: Rather like mountain lake spot

blocks.note: a tarn is a small upland lake
the suffix -ish means somewhat or rather like

explanation.surface: A hiker's view: a place resembling an upland pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' looks like a noun for a place; it is a verb, to stain. The suffix comes first in the clue but last in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarnish is to dull or stain a surface or reputation, and to spot something is likewise to mark or blemish it.

clue.text: Flipping retreat over current newspaper piece

indicators.note: flipping something turns it upside down, so the letters run back to front

blocks.note: a lair is a hideaway or retreat
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
a tide is a current of water

explanation.surface: An exasperated reporter complains about pulling out of a topical news story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' poses as a mild British curse word. 'Current' tempts you towards topical news, but it is a flow of water.
explanation.definitionFit: An editorial is an article giving the publication's own opinion, a standard item in a daily paper.

clue.text: Famous Miliband brother, David presumably?

blocks.note: the negative word: David is presumably the other brother, not the one named below
Ed Miliband, the former Labour leader

explanation.surface: A question about which of the well-known political Miliband brothers is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: David and Ed Miliband are British Labour politicians who ran against each other for the party leadership in 2010; David is, presumably, the one who is 'not Ed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means well known or celebrated, as in a noted author, a close synonym of famous.

clue.text: Look on face of Siamese cat Pete spoilt

indicators.note: a face is the front, so only the first letter is taken
something spoilt is ruined and out of shape, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the opening letter of Siamese
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone notes the expression on the face of a pampered Siamese cat called Pete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look on' seems to describe an expression on a face; it is the phrasal verb meaning watch.
explanation.definitionFit: To spectate is to watch an event as an onlooker without taking part, exactly what looking on means.

clue.text: Every second farm boy really lacking any principles

indicators.note: taking every second item means skipping one each time, so alternate letters are kept

blocks.note: the even-placed letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A rural lad is said to be truly unscrupulous.
explanation.walkthrough: Start with the second letter, A of fArm, and take every other letter through to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone amoral has no sense of right and wrong at all, so has no moral standards guiding conduct.
